catalog_quote: Orma has tone, but its functional load is minimal, and classifying it has been difficult. No function has been discovered that would require it to be marked in the Orma orthography. ... No minimal pairs have been found which are distinguished by tone. ... It has been difficult to classify Orma tone. The 1992 Phonology stated that although tone exists on various levels, the only functions which can be indicated solely by a difference in tone are focus in a simple sentence and the distinction between some case endings (p. 50). It concluded that Orma is not a pitch-accent language. ... However, in the 2005 Addendum, this conclusion was reversed ... Tone functions independently of stress.…The Orma data currently on hand tends to support the theory that Oromo languages may be more accurately described as pitch-accent languages, rather than tone languages. ... Therefore, the current hypothesis is that tone does serve some restrictive function in Orma, but that none are important enough to warrant marking it in the orthography.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (39 pp., text layer; extracted text copy). Locator verified by per-page extraction: '8. Tone' opens on PDF p. 35 (printed 34); '8.4 Classification' and the Payton 2005 block quote ('Tone functions independently of stress..The Orma data currently on hand tends to support the theory that Oromo languages may be more accurately described as pitch accent languages, rather than tone languages.') are on PDF p. 36 (printed 35). Every segment of the reported quote matches the text verbatim; the [..] gaps elide exactly 'No function has been discovered.. no interest has been expressed for marking tone.', the gender/syntax postulate sentence plus sections 8.1-8.3, and 'although tone exist…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only open first-hand description says Orma has (high) tone of minimal functional load -- no lexical minimal pairs, a marginal role in focus and in distinguishing benefactive (Adiá, final high) from source case (Adia) -- and that its classification (tone vs pitch accent, and its relation to stress) is unresolved; it gives NO rule for the position of word stress or accent. The placement rule itself is apparently stated in Stroomer 1987 (stress section pp. 30-36, mentions the penultimate syllable), which could not be opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone-bearing contrasts limited to: benefactive vs source case ending (Guyyonī Adiá barua barreessā 'for Adi' vs Adia 'from Adi'), focus in simple sentences (per Payton 1992 p. 50); glottal stop 'may occur word-finally on high tone syllables' (§3.2.5, p. 11). Tone plays no role in gender assignment (§8.1, §9.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone/accent discussed only functionally (orthography decision); no citation-form vs phrase distinction drawn. Hoskins's own current hypothesis (§8.4): 'tone does serve some restrictive function in Orma, but none important enough to warrant marking it in the orthography.'
new_statements.identity_note: Hoskins 2011 describes Tana River Orma (data mainly from Galole Division/Wayu village and later Tana River District work under BTL 1998-2007) = orma1241 proper. Hoskins (fn. 20) reports that local Waata (Sanye, separate ISO ssn / glottocode waat1238) and Orma speakers consider their languages identical, and quotes Heine 1981 on Waata tone; Heine 1980 'Munyo' is a Tana Orma variety filed by Glottolog under orma1241. Stroomer 1987 covers Orma together with Boraana (bora1271) and Waata.

sources.note: Section 8 'Tone' (pp. 34-35): Orma has tone but with minimal functional load, no tonal minimal pairs, not marked in orthography; tone marginally distinguishes benefactive vs source case (Adiá vs Adia) and focus; classification unresolved -- Payton 1992 said not pitch accent, Payton 2005 addendum reversed ('Tone functions independently of stress.. pitch accent'). No rule for where stress/accent falls is given anywhere in the paper; 'stress' otherwise appears only in an English diphthong aside and a footnote defining pitch accent.
